newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels throw down gauntlet to Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels throw down gauntlet to Fujimori.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Peru threw down the gauntlet on Monday to President Alberto Fujimori, saying there would be no further release of captives until the government sat down to negotiate their demands.

"There will be no more releases so long as the government fails to agree to a political solution," Isaac Velazco, the rebels' international spokesman, said in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.

He said a "political solution" would consist of sending his negotiator Domingo Palermo for talks inside the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador, where the rebels and hostages had been holed up for 20 days, and allowing rebels to communicate with their jailed comrades.
The rebels were demanding the release of some 400 imprisoned colleagues from Peruvian jails.
There was no response from the government. Fujimori met Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar, whose country's ambassador is among the hostages, but made no public statement.

At the besieged residence International Committee of the Red Cross officials made their routine visit to take in food and water but there was no sign of Michel Minnig, the top Red Cross official in the country and a key go-between in the crisis.

Witnesses said lights, presumably from lanterns or candles since electricity to the compound has been cut off, were seen at several windows but there were no other signs of activity inside and no repeat of a hearty round of singing heard Sunday.
Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori, also stayed away on Monday.
However a band of traditional Andean witchdoctors carrying skulls and potions went to the site and beseeched spirits to coax the rebels into freeing the captives.

A single face-to-face meeting on December 28 between Palermo and Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the rebel leader inside the compound, represented the start of negotiations, according to Velazco. But President Alberto Fujimori "broke" them off with his subsequent statements, he said.
In a speech on Thursday, Fujimori said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, whom he called "terrorists," were bent on pointless violence that served to increase poverty in Peru.
The rebels have not freed any hostages since that speech.
"We have made too many gestures. We have released many people without receiving a single response from the government," Velazco said.
The series of hostage releases -- in which the guerrillas freed more than 430 captives -- stopped after seven men were let out New Year's Day.

The deadlock sparked fears that one false move by the government or rebels could trigger a bloody end to the 20-day siege. In Tokyo Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned on Monday the standoff at the besieged residence could get out of hand.

"It will be a protracted battle and situations like that make me worried about an unexpected accident," he told reporters. "There have been miscues on the guerrillas' side and also on the Peruvian government's side," he added without elaborating.
The rebels mined and booby-trapped the residence in anticipation of any assault by government forces.
Cerpa was moving constantly around the building, using important hostages such as Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela as a "human shield," according to a local newspaper.

Peruvian intelligence officials were using a satellite to track movements inside the residence, the newspaper, Expreso, reported. The images showed the guerrillas operating a rotation system allowing five of them to sleep at any one time, for four hours each day, it reported from Washington, without specifying whether the surveillance satellite was American or Japanese.

While Japan urged Peru to look for a peaceful solution to the crisis, Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, rejected ruling out force until all hostages are released and the guerrillas lay down their arms.

The rebels are widely believed to number about 20 but the Red Cross fuelled speculation there could be more because the organisation provided those inside the residence with 110 portions for each meal -- 16 more than thought necessary.
The rebels burst in on a Dec(ember) 17 cocktail party honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday that was attended by more than 500 people.
